newsitem.title: USA: Saudi bomb suspect in U.S. is rethinking plea deal.
newsitem.headline: Saudi bomb suspect in U.S. is rethinking plea deal.

text.p: A Saudi suspect in the bombing that killed 19 U.S. airmen a year ago is reconsidering a plea bargain under which he was to have told U.S. officials all he knows about the attack, a lawyer said on Thursday.

U.S. District Court Judge Emmet Sullivan postponed proceedings until July 10 at the request of lawyers for the suspect, Hani al-Sayegh. Calling the case "unusual and complex," Sullivan agreed that a new court-appointed public defender, Francis Carter, needed time to prepare and familiarize Sayegh with his rights.

"Certain fundamental principles of the American justice system are not in the ordinary experience of my client," Carter told the court. His former co-counsel, Michael Wildes, said Sayegh, 29, was rethinking the deal under which he was deported to the United States from Canada 10 days ago.

"He is fearful that that he will be used as the basis for retaliation against a third country, namely, Iran," Wildes told Reuters before today's court appearance by Sayegh. "He clearly has problems with the agreement."

Wildes declined to elaborate because the proposed plea bargain remains under court seal. But he said Sayegh maintained he was not involved in any way in the June 25, 1996, attack on Khobar Towers in Dhahran that killed 19 U.S. Air Force members and injured 500.

Under the deal, Sayegh was to have pleaded guilty to conspiracy to commit murder in an earlier, abortive alleged anti-American plot in Saudi Arabia. In exchange for a reduced sentence on that charge, he had been expected to tell U.S. officials everything he knew about the Khobar attack.
Sayegh has been identified in Canadian court documents as the driver of a car that flashed a go-ahead signal for the bomb-laden truck involved at Khobar, a charge he denies.

Wildes said Sayegh, who is being held in a safe house at an undisclosed location, maintained he was not involved in any way in the bombing. Sayegh says witnesses will place him in the holy city of Qum in Iran when the attack took place.

"He has no information whatsoever, at all, as to who perpetrated this atrocity or any details in this regard," said Wildes, who no longer represents Sayegh in the criminal case but continues as his immigration counsel and adviser.
Sayegh was deported on June 17 from Canada, where he was arrested in March on charges of posing a security risk. He was indicted in Washington on the conspiracy charge the next day.

A U.S. federal grand jury charged that Sayegh, a Shi'ite Moslem described in Canadian court documents as a member of Saudi Hizbollah, was associated with a "terrorist" group that it did not name. Saudi Hizbollah, or Party of God, is a militant group backed by Iran.

Sullivan said on Thursday a court-ordered medical examination of Sayegh had found nothing to keep him from taking part in the case. Proceedings were postponed last week after Sayegh had an asthma attack.
As he entered the courtroom wearing a black T-shirt, Sayegh grinned and waved jauntily to spectators from behind a 10-foot-high bulletproof plastic partition.
